newsitem.title: JAPAN: E.Asia Oilseeds - Japan, Korea buying U.S. soybeans.
newsitem.headline: E.Asia Oilseeds - Japan, Korea buying U.S. soybeans.

text.p: Japanese and South Korean buyers said they plan to buy U.S. soybeans this week, while Taiwan is expected to tender for up to 108,000 tonnes of soybeans from the U.S., Brazil or Argentina, regional traders said on Monday.
"We've finished buying U.S. soybeans for April shipment, and are now covering for early May shipment," a soybean trader in Tokyo said.
The Japanese are carefully watching to see if Brazil will impose an export tax on soybeans.
Chicago soybean futures ended sharply higher on Friday, as funds bought at least 20 million bushels of soybeans amid rumours Brazil would impose a three percent export tax.
Traders on the Chicago Board of Trade (COBT) have said such a tax would raise Brazilian export prices and encourage buyers to puchase U.S.-origin beans.
A Taiwanese soybean buyer said, however, that any increase in the export tax should have little real impact in the market.
"Even if Brazil did add a tariff, it's likely be only three percent and that has little impact on the competitiveness of Brazilian soybeans," a buyer at Taiwan's Hui Shung Group said.
"For Brazilian crop, we've already covered until August shipment. Our buying pace (for Brazilian origin) is quicker than usual this year," a trader in Japan added.
Dealers said Japan has bought up to 800,000 tonnes of Brazilian soybeans so far this season and Japan will seek U.S. beans if Brazil actually resorts to the export levy.

China and Japanese trade houses are also starting negotiations over soybean exports to Japan for the May-September 1997 period in Beijing, traders said. Chinese soybeans are mainly used for making miso or soybean paste here.
"Some miso makers are still sticking to Chinese soybean, and are ready to buy if its prices are competitive against U.S.," a Tokyo soybean trader said.
The Japanese are expected to ask Chinese suppliers to keep soybean prices unchanged from the January-April period at nearly US$395 a tonne on an FOB basis, traders said.
In South Korea, feed milling companies were said to be seeking oilseeds this week instead of corn -- due to recent high prices for the grain, traders said.
The Feed Buying Group on Monday invited tenders for 26,500 tonnes of rapeseed meal and 36,000 tonnes of wheatbran pellet by 0300 GMT on Tuesday.
Traders said another group of buyers called the Big Feed Mills are also expected to seek tapioca and soymeal this week.
South Korean edible oil producers are also seen buying 50,000 tonnes of U.S. No.2 soybean for shipment in April.
In Taiwan, traders are expected to see two tenders this week for up to 108,000 tonnes soybeans with the supply probably coming from the United States, Brazil or Argentina.
Taiwanese interest in Brazilian and Argentine soybeans remains strong as buyers seek alternatives to bypass strong U.S. soybean futures prices, they said.
Buyers in Taiwan would consider buying Argentine soybeans if prices were $10 or more below that of the United States.
Brazilian soybeans, which are seen as of higher quality than Argentine beans, would be considered at prices similar to U.S. prices.
Members of Taiwan's Breakfast Soybean Procurement Association Kaohsiung division will send delegates to Brazil in April to review the country's crop, silo facilities and port conditions.
